Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 63
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Auditor
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 63

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Locked Spaces: Being in a locked or confined room, Being in Nature: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened, Victim Memories: Reminders of victims
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Vignette:
Samira stood at the threshold of the conference room, her palm resting on the heavy steel door. When the latch clicked shut, the sudden quiet folded around her like a thick wool coat. She was no longer in the suburban office park where she audited quarterly financials for mid-sized firms; she was back in the botanical preserve, ten years gone, watching her husband’s body go slack against the oak roots. The memory did not visit as a passing picture or a distant story. It arrived fully, a complete sensory sweep: the damp earth smell, the coarse bark against her fingers, the sharp copper taste of his sudden collapse, and the overwhelming terror that had gripped her chest in that exact, unyielding second. Her body, even now, stayed in that state of alarm, muscles coiled as if the path behind her might still give way. In the years since, Samira had built a careful architecture around her days. She avoided unfamiliar places. She could not assess the danger when the terrain shifted, so she drove familiar routes, booked the same hotel chains, and turned back when the pavement grew unfamiliar. Her sleep grew fractured. She would lie awake in the dark, listening to the house settle, convinced the floorboards carried the same warning creak she had heard in the preserve. Her body kept reacting as though the threat had never passed, every minor sound or change of light drawing her into a state of watchful readiness. She could not stop bad things from happening. She had come to believe that misfortune waited in any unguarded moment, and that her own measures were ultimately thin against it. She had lost faith, slowly, in the steady order of things, in the reliability of those around her, and in the higher power she used to pray to for quiet evenings. These shifts in her world did not arrive with fanfare, but settled like dust, layer upon layer, until the familiar no longer felt quite as safe. The auditor’s life demanded movement, which meant new rooms and shifting horizons. During a routine site visit last month, she sat in a windowless meeting room reviewing ledger books when the air conditioning hummed a familiar low note. Without warning, the room felt utterly confined, the walls pressing in like the tree line of the preserve. The door latch clicked. Samira’s breath shortened. She saw the other staff members as victims in passing, their sudden coughs or slumped postures mirroring the way her husband had fallen. She had learned to step back, to keep her distance, letting the world move through her while she remained anchored to the known. Her audits continued, but she now carried the room’s quiet confinement with her into every new assessment. At sixty-three, single, and resting on a PCL5 score of sixty-three, Samira found herself standing at the end of her tether. The habits had accumulated over months, then years, into a quiet exhaustion. She no longer bristled at the triggers; she simply accepted them as part of the landscape. What finally brought her to seek help was not a single crisis, but the steady weight of days that no longer felt secure. She wanted to know how to live in a world that still held locked doors and unfamiliar paths, and whether the terror that lived in her chest could be trusted to settle, even as her body continued to watch.
